indicators.note: jazzy suggests something lively and improvised, so the letters are freely rearranged

explanation.surface: Duke Ellington's lively diet nourishes the soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jazzy' shuffles DIET and SOUL together. The definition is just 'Ellington's', meaning a piece by Duke Ellington, one of several jazz standards in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitude is a 1934 jazz standard composed by Duke Ellington, so it is one of Ellington's works.

clue.text: Carmichael's beginning to impress Duke and the Guardian

indicators.note: to impress is to press something into another, so the start word takes the other pieces inside it

parts.note: a beginning is a start
the setter writes for the Guardian newspaper, so the paper speaks of itself as us

explanation.surface: Hoagy Carmichael begins to make an impression on Duke Ellington and this newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' reads like part of 'Carmichael's beginning', but it is the outer word, and 'to impress' is the container signal. 'Carmichael's' alone is the definition: a song by Hoagy Carmichael.
explanation.definitionFit: Stardust is Hoagy Carmichael's best-known song, a 1927 jazz standard.

clue.text: Second offensive finally penetrating slack base

indicators.note: penetrating means going into, so the last letter enters the other piece

parts.note: slack means idle or indolent, in a word lazy

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word offensive

explanation.surface: A second attack eventually breaks through a slack defensive base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' gives S; 'finally' takes the E of offensive, and 'penetrating' puts it inside LAZY.
explanation.definitionFit: Base here is an adjective meaning low or sordid, which is close to seedy and disreputable.

clue.text: Cannons finding the opposite for Antipodeans, one and all?

parts.note: Australians and New Zealanders call an English person, someone from the opposite side of the world, a pom
all of the English, to an Antipodean, are poms

explanation.surface: Cannon fire meets its opposite number among the Australians, every single one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: POM is Australian slang for an English person; one gives POM and all of them POMS. A pom-pom is a quick-firing automatic cannon.
explanation.definitionFit: A pom-pom is a rapid-firing anti-aircraft autocannon, named for the sound of its shots, so these are cannons.

clue.text: Fabric has to fade beneath instrument

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath places the fading word below the instrument

parts.note: an organ is a musical instrument
to die away is to fade

explanation.surface: A fabric starts to lose its colour underneath an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'beneath' puts DIE under ORGAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Organdie is a fine, stiff, translucent cotton fabric, spelt organdy in American English.

clue.text: Cross about fairy heading for Oberon in condescending manner

indicators.note: about means around, so the bad-tempered word goes round the other pieces

parts.note: cross means bad-tempered, which is surly
a peri is a fairy or sprite in Persian myth

indicators.note: heading for takes the first letter of Oberon

explanation.surface: Someone irritable about a fairy goes to see Oberon, the fairy king, in a lofty way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb but is the adjective meaning bad-tempered; 'about' is the container signal and 'heading for' picks Oberon's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting superiorly means behaving as though better than others, which is a condescending manner.

clue.text: Quite unusual to have half of food before meal

indicators.note: before puts the half first, ahead of the meal
half of takes the second two of the four letters of food

parts.note: a dish is a meal or a course

explanation.surface: It is rather odd to eat half your food before the main course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes the back half of food, and 'before' places it ahead of the meal word.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish means somewhat, so a slightly odd thing is quite unusual.

clue.text: Instrument entertaining big time, as half of a double act

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting, so the instrument holds the other pieces inside

parts.note: a cello is a stringed instrument
OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for big

explanation.surface: A musician's instrument is a big hit, like one half of a comedy partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertaining' is the container signal. Lou Costello was the partner of Bud Abbott in the American comedy duo Abbott and Costello.
explanation.definitionFit: Lou Costello formed the double act Abbott and Costello, making him half of it.

parts.note: the figure 0 is a round shape
twelve on the clock at night is midnight

explanation.surface: A monk's numerical puzzle of zero over twelve.
explanation.walkthrough: Thelonious Monk's jazz standard is written 'Round Midnight; the zero is ROUND and twelve is MIDNIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Round Midnight is a 1944 jazz standard by the pianist Thelonious Monk, so it is one of Monk's pieces.

indicators.note: gutted means the insides are removed, here the central letter

parts.note: a tiger is a big cat; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A quarrel in which the cat is disembowelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' removes the middle G of TIGER. 'Row' looks like a quarrel, but it means a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one of a series of rows placed one above another, as in a theatre.

clue.text: Place in a mess with habit of every character

indicators.note: in a mess means untidy and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Put something in a muddle along with a monk's habit belonging to every person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a mess' shuffles PLACE and HABIT together. 'character' means a letter of the alphabet, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphabetic describes something involving the alphabet, the set of every written character.

clue.text: Exposure, as opposed to either 9 14, 17 26, 23, 1, 2 24 or 22 15, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear means the clue's phrase is spoken aloud and matched to a word with the same sound

parts.note: all the cross-referenced entries are old jazz standards, so something unlike them is a new ditty, a fresh little song

explanation.surface: Being exposed rather than wearing any of the old standards in the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The referenced entries are old jazz songs, so the opposite is a NEW DITTY, which 'we hear' says sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudity is being naked, a state of complete exposure.

indicators.note: eaten by means swallowed up, so the passport goes inside the friendly word

parts.note: intimate means close and friendly
a passport is a form of ID or identification

explanation.surface: A passport has been chewed up by a docile cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten by' is the container signal. 'cow' is a verb meaning to frighten into submission, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to bully them into submission, which is to frighten or overawe.

parts.note: making peace ends something, so end is the first part
what peace ends is the anger, the bad feeling between people

explanation.surface: A question of whether a threat might be a way to make peace.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as END ANGER, which is what making peace does.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger something is to put it at risk, which is to threaten it.

clue.text: Carmichael's upsetting moggy with Iron Maiden

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over and into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Hoagy Carmichael is offended by a pet cat accompanied by a heavy metal band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' shuffles MOGGY (British slang for a cat) and IRON MAIDEN together; 'with' only joins them. Iron Maiden is a British heavy metal band.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgia on My Mind is a 1930 song by Hoagy Carmichael, later famously recorded by Ray Charles.

clue.text: Division of legion is in goal, charging

indicators.note: Division of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of the legion is in goal, attacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charging' looks like a military rush, but it means giving an electric charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionising means turning atoms into ions, which gives them an electric charge.

clue.text: A loop securing the last of your fruit

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the loop wraps round the final letter

parts.note: a picot is a small decorative loop on lace or ribbon

indicators.note: the last of takes the final letter of the word your

explanation.surface: A loop fastening the remains of your fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the last of' gives R from your; 'securing' puts it inside PICOT, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a soft orange stone fruit related to the plum.

clue.text: Fighting, setter gets dessert back out of the oven again

parts.note: fighting is war
the setter refers to himself as me

indicators.note: back means the dessert word is read from right to left

parts.note: pud is short for pudding, a British word for dessert

explanation.surface: In a battle, the setter receives a pudding fresh from a second baking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PUD into DUP. PUD is British informal for pudding, i.e. dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Food warmed up has been reheated, taken out of the oven a second time.

parts.note: a mount is a horse for riding

explanation.surface: A question about the price of a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking how much asks for an amount, a quantity or total.

indicators.note: cutting means going into, so always goes inside the grass word

parts.note: to grass, British slang for informing on someone, is to sing
ay (or aye) is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A saw is forever slicing through the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' is the container signal. 'Saw' is a proverb, not the tool, and 'grass' is the British slang verb to inform on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old proverb or maxim, which is a saying.

definitions.meaning: a song by the American composer Harold Arlen, from 1933
a tempest is a violent storm, so the title describes rough conditions outside

explanation.surface: Harold Arlen's version of the Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's play is a decoy: the quoted title is just a tempest, a violent storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormy Weather is a 1933 song by Harold Arlen, and a tempest is literally a spell of violent storm.

parts.note: to low is to moo, the sound cattle make

indicators.note: biting means holding in the teeth, so the dog surrounds the princess

parts.note: a dingo is a wild Australian dog
Di is short for Diana, Princess of Wales

explanation.surface: Ellington's lowly dog takes a bite at a princess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biting' is the container signal, the dog holding the princess. 'low' is the cattle sound, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Mood Indigo is a 1930 jazz standard by Duke Ellington, so it is one of Ellington's works.

parts.note: a dam is a barrier across water

indicators.note: beginning to takes the first letter of erode

explanation.surface: A wide barrier starts to wear away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broad' is American slang for a woman, not wide.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame and broad are both slang for a woman, chiefly American.

parts.note: a nit, short for nitwit, is a fool
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: An idiot fools around near the gunpowder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre is potassium nitrate, saltpetre, a key ingredient of gunpowder.
